opus-5.5.text:
I think this is one of the most important questions right now, and my view might be a bit different from the mainstream.

Today, the large language model sits at the center of almost every AI system. Vision, audio, and everything else get treated as add-ons. You take an image, run it through an encoder, project it into the language model's token space, and let the LLM do the "real" thinking. Language has become the hub and every other modality a spoke.

I don't think that's the final form. Language is an incredibly powerful interface. It's compressed, it's symbolic, and it's how humans communicate and pass on knowledge. But it is a very lossy description of the world. Much of what intelligence needs, like spatial understanding, physical intuition, how objects move and interact, and what happens when you push something, isn't well captured in text. Humans and animals build most of that understanding before language, or entirely without it. A cat has a very good world model and doesn't speak a single word.

So when I think about representation learning, I'm thinking about how we learn good internal representations of the world directly from sensory data, mostly visual data, at scale. If we get that right, I think the role of the LLM shifts. Instead of being the brain that everything else feeds into, language becomes one interface on top of a richer representational substrate. It's very good for communication, for reasoning over abstractions, and for planning in a symbolic way. But the grounding, the actual model of how the world works, would come from somewhere else.

You can already see hints of this. In many multimodal models, the vision part is surprisingly weak. They can describe an image fluently, but if you ask very basic visual questions, like counting, spatial relationships, or fine-grained details, they fail in ways a child wouldn't. Part of the reason is that the visual representations were never really learned for understanding the world. They were learned to align with text. So the system inherits language's blind spots.

I think the next phase will push in a few directions. First, visual representation learning that isn't purely supervised by language. Self-supervised learning, learning from video, learning from interaction. Second, architectures where the representation space isn't forced to be the language token space. Maybe there's a shared latent space where language, vision, and action all live as first-class citizens. Third, connecting this to world models and embodied systems, where the model has to predict and act, not just describe.

In that picture, the LLM doesn't disappear. It's still extremely useful. But I'd describe it more as the "mouth" of the system, or maybe part of the reasoning layer, rather than the whole brain. The foundation underneath, the representations of the physical world, is where I think a lot of the progress over the next few years will come from. Honestly, as someone who works in vision, I think this is a very exciting time. It feels like vision is about to have its moment again, but in a quite different form than before.

r001.rationale: The response argues for learning rich representations of the world, but does not say that a sufficiently good representation makes downstream problems easy to solve.

r002.rationale: It describes language as an interface on top of a richer representational substrate and calls the LLM the system’s “mouth” or part of its reasoning layer.

r003.rationale: It mentions a possible shared latent space, but does not propose a cognitive architecture of interconnected neural modules rather than a single model checkpoint.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this is actually one of the most important questions in the field right now, and my view has shifted quite a bit over the past couple of years.

For a long time, the dominant narrative was that language models would be the center of everything. You scale up a transformer on text, and then you bolt on vision, audio, action, whatever you need, and the LLM acts as the brain. And honestly, that worked surprisingly well. But when we actually dug into what these models learn, especially on the visual side, we found the picture is more complicated than "the language model understands everything."

What I've come to believe is that language is a very lossy interface to the world. It's an incredible compression, and it's been amazing as a training signal because the internet gave us so much of it. But a lot of what matters about the world, spatial structure, physics, how objects move and interact, fine-grained visual detail, none of that lives naturally in text. If you only learn representations through the lens of language, you inherit the blind spots of language.

So the shift I see is that representation learning stops being a preprocessing step that feeds the LLM and becomes a first-class citizen. Right now, in most multimodal systems, the vision encoder is a frozen thing trained with some contrastive objective, and the LLM is trying to make sense of whatever features come out of it. When we did careful studies on this, we saw that a lot of failure modes in multimodal models traced directly back to the visual representation, not to the language model. The LLM is smart, but it can't recover information the encoder never captured.

In the future, I think the LLM becomes one component rather than the center. It's extremely good at reasoning, at planning, at interfacing with humans, at retrieving knowledge. But the world model, the part that actually understands how things look and how they evolve over time, will come from representations learned directly from visual and sensory data, possibly from video at massive scale, possibly from generative objectives rather than purely discriminative ones. And there's a genuine open question about whether those representations should even be aligned to language early on, or whether that alignment should happen late, after the visual side has learned its own structure.

There's also a more philosophical point. We've been in a regime where scaling the LLM gave you better everything, so representation learning felt almost solved by default. I think that era is ending. The marginal returns from text are flattening, and the next big gains will come from learning better representations of modalities where we haven't yet found the right objective. That's actually exciting for someone like me, because it means the core research questions about what makes a good representation are back at the center of the field rather than hidden behind the language model.

So to put it simply: I don't think LLMs go away. I think they move from being the whole system to being the reasoning and communication layer on top of representations that are learned much more directly from the world.

r001.rationale: The response says better representations can capture information the LLM lacks, but does not argue that a sufficiently good representation makes downstream problems easy to solve.

r002.rationale: It predicts LLMs will serve as a reasoning and communication layer on top of representations learned directly from the world.

r003.rationale: It describes the LLM as one component and a separate world model, but does not suggest that the world model is an interconnected neural architecture rather than a single checkpoint.

astra-6.text:
I think representation learning will remain central, even if the interface to these systems is language. Language gives us a powerful way to communicate and organize knowledge, but it doesn’t capture everything about the world. There’s a lot in visual experience, motion, and physical interaction that is difficult to express fully in words.

So one possibility is that large language models become part of a broader system that learns from all these sources. The important question is how those representations connect. Can the system connect what it sees to what it says, and then use that understanding to decide what to do? Simply adding an image encoder to a language model doesn’t necessarily solve that.

I also wouldn’t assume we already know the right architecture. A unified model might learn these capabilities together, or different components might learn complementary representations. What matters is whether those representations support generalization—whether the system can handle a new situation rather than just produce a plausible description of it.

In that sense, representation learning could shift the role of language models from primarily generating answers toward participating in systems with a more grounded understanding of the world.

r001.rationale: The response says representations should support generalization, but does not argue that a sufficiently good learned representation makes downstream problems easy to solve.

r002.rationale: It describes language as a way to communicate and says language models may participate in broader grounded systems, but does not predict that they will serve as communication interfaces to an underlying representation or world model.

r003.rationale: It allows for different components to learn complementary representations, but does not identify the foundational world model as a cognitive architecture of interconnected neural modules.

sol-6.1.text:
I think representation learning will remain fundamental. A language model is already learning representations, but language is only one view of the world. The interesting question is how we connect that view with vision, action, and experience.

For example, a model might describe an object very well without understanding what happens when you push it or look at it from another angle. Learning from those interactions could give us representations that capture more of the underlying structure, beyond what people have written down.

So I could imagine language models becoming one component of a broader system. Language would be a powerful interface for communication and reasoning, while other components help the system perceive, predict, and act. Whether those components eventually become one unified model is still an open question.

The key is whether the representations support learning new tasks and generalizing to unfamiliar situations. Better language generation alone doesn’t necessarily tell us that.

r001.rationale: The response says representations should support learning new tasks and generalization, but does not claim that a sufficiently good representation makes downstream problems easy to solve.

r002.rationale: It describes language as a powerful interface for communication and reasoning within a broader system whose other components perceive, predict, and act, alongside representations of underlying structure.

r003.rationale: It leaves open whether components will unify, but does not propose an interconnected neural-module cognitive architecture as the foundational world model.
